title: The chariot
hookLine: is the chariot the axle, the wheels, the pole? "Nagasena" is a name for parts together (Milinda, Book 2)

lines: ONLY A NAME, A WAY OF SPEAKING.
cards: The king asks the simplest question there is: what's your name? The monk's answer surprises the court. He's called Nagasena, he says; that's what his parents and fellow monks call him.
But it's only a name, a way of speaking. No lasting person is found behind it. The king turns to his courtiers, half amused, half offended.
If there's no person here, who wears these robes? Who keeps the rules? Who gets the credit when someone gives alms, and who's to blame if someone harms you?
Nagasena doesn't argue. He asks the king how he got here today.

teach.h: IS THE POLE THE CHARIOT? THE WHEELS?
teach.b: First, the chariot at the door. The king came by chariot, so Nagasena asks him to point to it. Is the pole the chariot?
The frame, the yoke, the reins? No, no, no. All of these together?
No. Something apart from them? No again.
Second, the turn. Then there is no chariot, Nagasena says, and the king has told a falsehood in front of his court. The courtiers cheer for the monk.

teach.h: THE KING WORKS IT OUT ALOUD.
teach.b: And the king, to his credit, works it out aloud. He hasn't lied: chariot is the name used for the pole, the axle, the wheels, the frame and the rest, when they come together. Third, the point.

teach.h: NAGASENA: A NAME FOR PARTS TOGETHER.
teach.b: Just so, Nagasena says: Nagasena is the name for this body, these feelings, perceptions, mental formations and consciousness, when they come together. Nothing is hidden behind the parts; the name is real as a name.
He recalls a verse of the nun Vajira, from the older suttas: where the parts are gathered, people say chariot; where the parts of a life are present, people say a being. The king praises the answer.
Fourth, what this doesn't say. It doesn't say Nagasena isn't there, or that names are lies.

teach.h: THE CHARIOT STILL CARRIES HIM HOME.
teach.b: The king still rides home in his chariot.
A name points to parts working together, not to a fixed core inside them. Buddhists call this anatta, not-self, and this simile is one of the ways teachers still explain it.

how: Buddhist teachers often use the chariot simile from the Questions of King Milinda, together with the nun Vajira's verse, to explain not-self: a name is used for parts working together, with no fixed core behind them.

o: a soul that rides inside the body, like a driver
proof that names, and the people they name, are lies
a name for parts working together, not a hidden core

p: the pole, the axle, the wheels
none of them alone is the chariot
a name for the parts together
a name for body, feeling, mind together
the nun whose verse Nagasena recalls

s: Nagasena says he doesn't exist at all
he says Nagasena is a name used for the parts of a life together, with no fixed person behind them.
the king first concludes that the chariot is all its parts together
he says no to every part and to all of them together, then realizes chariot is the name used when they come together.
Nagasena backs his point with a verse from a nun
he recalls the nun Vajira's verse: where the parts are gathered, people say chariot.

games.q: you're the king. you rode here by chariot, and the monk has made you deny that the pole, the wheels, and every other part is the chariot. what do you say?
o: fine, then there is no chariot.
the chariot is a hidden thing beyond the parts.
chariot is the name used for the parts together.
games.why: the king works it out: he hasn't lied, because chariot is the name used when the parts come together. Nagasena says, just so with his own name.

practice: Pick something near you, a cup, a chair, a phone, and name its parts slowly: the handle, the rim, the base. Where among them is the cup itself?
Then gently turn the same question toward your own name, a body breathing, feelings coming and going, thoughts, and just watch the parts working together, with no conclusion needed.

wordCard.voice: The chariot. Nagasena's simile: not the pole, not the wheels, nothing apart from them; chariot is a name for the parts together.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: chariot. the simile Nagasena uses for his own name.

carryVoice: Your line: a name for parts. The chariot still gets the king home. Day eight hundred sixty-eight, and another week behind us.
